video_title: From Crimea to Kostiantynivka - Logistics Strikes & Ukraine's Fortress Belt
gist: At the 2026 halfway point, Perun argues Russia's infiltration-plus-fires offensive model is delivering far less territory than in 2025 (~10 sq mi net May-June, with ISW scoring it net negative) while Ukraine fights 'around the problem' with mid- and long-range drone strikes on Russian logistics, refineries, bridges and space-control facilities. The two case studies are Kostyantynivka, where Russia is slowly unravelling a fortress-belt city after ~8 months, and Crimea, where a compounding fuel and bridge-interdiction squeeze has pushed the Russian governor to declare a state of emergency.

insights.claim: Russia's net territorial gain between May and June 2026 was roughly 10 square miles on one open-source mapping tool — less than half the area of Manhattan — while ISW scored Russia net negative for the same period.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Territorial-rate data is the cleanest public metric for whether Russian offensive claims are credible; a glacial rate undercuts the assumption that Donbas objectives fall on any near-term timeline.
insights.quote: Russia's net territorial gain for the month from May to June 2026 was about 10 square miles, less than half the size of Manhattan Island.

insights.claim: Despite the usual expectation that better weather plus political necessity would produce a scaled-up Russian offensive in 2026, no across-the-board sledgehammer offensive has materialised; Russian effort has instead been narrower and more focused on selected sectors.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Narrow-focus offensives imply Russia is resource-constrained rather than choosing restraint, which changes the read on how much reserve capacity exists for a later push.

insights.claim: Perun argues Russian military planning is partly hostage to an internal incentive trap: commanders overstate advances to the public and Putin, then must advance to match the claims, while promising the leadership that a bit more funding, time, recruits and drones will finally deliver the stated objectives.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: If reporting-driven sunk-cost dynamics rather than achievable objectives are setting Russian operational tempo, expect continued costly attacks even where the military math is poor.

insights.claim: By most metrics the front line in the first half of 2026 appears more stable than in the equivalent period of 2025, with Ukraine having pulled the balance somewhat back in its favour.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Front stability plus deep-strike escalation is the combination that would most raise the odds of Russia's cost calculus shifting.

themes.theme: Evolution and limits of Russian infiltration tactics

insights.claim: Russian assault tactics evolved in stages — massed mechanized columns, then dismounted infantry assaults, then infiltration by ones and twos — with each shift driven by the previous method's vulnerability to observation drones, mines and drone-corrected artillery.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A reusable model for reading future adaptations: the tactic that dominates is the one that best evades the current dominant sensor-shooter pairing, not the one that is most militarily elegant.

insights.claim: Infiltration works partly on economics: one or two infantrymen are usually not worth the artillery ammunition needed to eliminate them, which is why the burden has shifted onto FPV drones.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Explains why FPV production volume, not shell counts, is now the binding constraint on Ukraine's ability to hold the gray zone.

insights.claim: Perun likens Russian infiltration to playing Minesweeper — probing the weakest Ukrainian frontline points, rerouting each successive pair after a group is stopped, until infantry filter through and accumulate behind the lines for assault actions.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A probing model means defensive success depends on uniform line density and detection, not on holding a few strongpoints well.
insights.quote: The Russians, for lack of a better term, could almost play this like Minesweeper.

insights.claim: Infiltration teams have little organic combat power and fail when their three enabling conditions break: they can no longer cause panic, ambush supply lines effectively, or accumulate before clearing operations reach them.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete checklist for judging whether a given sector's defence will hold against infiltration pressure.

insights.claim: Ukrainian units have psychologically normalised infiltration, adopting a posture of holding position and readjusting logistics rather than panicking when Russian infantry appear in their rear.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The tactic's main effect was psychological dislocation; once that decays, its territorial yield falls even if its inputs are unchanged.
insights.quote: The understanding now often seems to be the gray zone is the gray zone, positions might be intermingled

insights.claim: Ukrainian reconnaissance units have increasingly pivoted away from reconnaissance — now largely done by drones — into dedicated clearing and anti-infiltration roles, alongside Ukraine's switch to the corps system.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Force-structure repurposing is a leading indicator that drones have absorbed a mission set; watch for similar reallocation in artillery and engineering units.

insights.claim: Lost Armor data on claimed Lancet loitering-munition hits shows rapid growth from 2022 to 2024, then a flattening and a recent decline to roughly 2023 levels — despite higher production, better guidance, larger warheads and claimed range extensions.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A Russian-sourced dataset showing declining claimed effectiveness is unusually credible evidence that Ukrainian counter-drone measures are working.

insights.claim: About half of Ukraine's visually confirmed self-propelled gun losses this year are the shorter-ranged 122mm 2S1, suggesting Russian unmanned systems threaten artillery close to the front far more than longer-range systems firing from depth.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Implies survivability is bought by range: longer-ranged Western and Ukrainian SPGs firing from depth remain comparatively safe, a live procurement argument.

insights.claim: The mid-range Russian strike threat that Ukrainians feared at the end of 2025 has not materialised as expected, with intense Russian activity concentrated within a couple of dozen kilometres of the front, attributed to Russia's loss of Starlink-equivalent connectivity and Ukraine's interceptor drones.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Cheap, reliable long-range connectivity — not airframes — is the decisive input; watch Russian satcom progress as the key unlock variable.

insights.claim: Kostyantynivka is the southern tip of Ukraine's Donbas fortress belt, sitting furthest south and east so it protrudes from the rest of the defensive position, with its primary supply line reduced to a single road connecting it to Druzhkivka.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Single-road dependency is the structural vulnerability that makes drone interdiction, rather than assault, the decisive Russian method here.

insights.claim: Rather than storming Kostyantynivka, Russia has expanded the gray zone around and into the city with drone operators suppressing resupply and infiltration teams working around the town, degrading Ukrainian defensive cohesion.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Urban objectives now fall by logistics strangulation rather than assault, so watch supply-road status, not frontline maps, to time a city's fall.

insights.claim: Perun's most likely expectation is that Russia eventually pushes Ukrainian forces out of Kostyantynivka, after which the city stays in the gray zone until Russia can move drone operators forward and push the kill zone back.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Capture would not immediately unlock further advance — the operational pause afterwards is where Ukraine gets time to re-set the next defensive line.

insights.claim: The battle for Kostyantynivka is generally accepted to have started around October 2025, meaning Russia has spent roughly eight months without fully taking the objective — a rate that, extrapolated, implies Ukraine can frustrate Russian Donbas ambitions for years.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The single best time-based benchmark in the episode for pricing how long a negotiated-settlement clock could run.
insights.quote: suggesting it's taken the Russians the better part of 8 months to not entirely take this objective

insights.claim: Ukrainian troops rotating out of forward Kostyantynivka positions carry a shotgun alongside the assault rifle — in one case two primary weapons at once — because the Russian FPV drone force in that sector is massive and dangerous.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Small-arms load-out changes are a ground-truth signal of local drone density that no claimed statistic can fake.
insights.quote: This is not something Ukrainian troops are likely doing because carrying several kilograms of additional weapon system and ammo is character building.

insights.claim: One Ukrainian soldier interviewed in a recent documentary rotated out of a forward position after 93 days, against a First World War British benchmark of roughly 3 to 6 days on the firing line with regular rotations out of the trench system.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Rotation length is a hard proxy for manpower strain and unit degradation in Ukraine's most contested sectors.

themes.theme: Logistics architecture and the layered supply chain

insights.claim: Ukrainian contested-area logistics now run a three-stage relay: trucks to a UGV position, UGVs to a heavy drone position, then heavy drones dropping food, water and ammunition into forward positions so no vehicle has to reach the frontline trench.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A transferable model for contested logistics that shifts demand from vehicles toward batteries, munitions and unmanned platforms at each handoff node.

insights.claim: The drone-relay logistics model breaks down for cargo a rotor drone cannot carry — medical evacuation in particular — and is not universal, with Ukrainian troops still moving supplies by handcart and heavy ruck.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Medevac is the unsolved gap in the unmanned logistics stack and the likely next demand pull for heavy-lift or ground autonomous systems.

insights.claim: Perun argues logistics UGVs should be built as cheap and attritable as possible, since a destroyed cargo UGV that carried more than several infantrymen's loads may still have done its job by substituting for exposed soldiers.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Argues against gold-plating ground robots — unit cost and production volume, not survivability, is the design axis that pays.
insights.quote: each one that cops a drone might be a Ukrainian infantryman that doesn't

themes.theme: Casualty ratios and the medevac asymmetry

insights.claim: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a Senate hearing that the Pentagon assessed for the first time that Russian killed in action was starting to outnumber Russian wounded — a ratio Perun notes would be remarkable by historical standards, worse than pre-penicillin World War I Western Front outcomes.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: An official US casualty-ratio assessment is a rare hard input for modelling Russian manpower burn and its political ceiling.
insights.quote: The number of Russian fatalities has exceeded the number of wounded, so the Ukrainians are not only fighting bravely, they're fighting effectively.

insights.claim: Perun explains an extreme Russian killed-to-wounded ratio not by an absent medical system but by where casualties occur: infiltrating Russian infantry are hit in no-man's-land or behind Ukrainian lines with no realistic evacuation, while many Ukrainian casualties are support elements behind the front with reasonable medevac chances.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A geometry-based explanation means the ratio is a structural consequence of infiltration doctrine and will persist as long as the doctrine does.

insights.claim: Perun highlights that both armies are demographically old, so wounded soldiers in their 40s or 50s with pre-existing conditions handle a long self-evacuation far worse than a 19 or 20-year-old would.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Demographics amplify the lethality of manpower-intensive tactics, worsening the true cost of each infiltration attempt beyond headline casualty counts.

themes.theme: Russian adaptation and the manpower math

insights.claim: Russia is beginning to add hard-kill protection to logistics vehicles — such as an escort technical with a machine gunner — because electronic warfare is unreliable against Ukrainian drones with AI terminal guidance, and Perun expects this effort to scale rather than peter out.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: AI terminal guidance breaking EW is the mechanism forcing a costly shift to kinetic convoy defence — a growth area for counter-UAS hardware on both sides.

insights.claim: Russia has been conducting mid-range strikes on Ukrainian gas stations, which are logistically important but do not demand the dynamic targeting capability needed to hit a moving truck or train.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Target selection reveals capability gaps: static-target preference indicates Russia still lacks Ukraine's real-time dynamic targeting chain.

insights.claim: Russia's constraint on mid-range strike is not the airframe — it already has platforms with range comparable to the Hornet or FP-02 — but matching Ukraine's affordable, reliable long-range communications provided by Starlink.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Identifies satellite connectivity as the single decisive bottleneck; Russian progress there would be the biggest negative inflection for Ukraine's rear areas.

insights.claim: Russia launched the first 16 satellites of its Rassvet constellation on March 23rd, of which 15 remain in orbit after one suffered orbital decay, with each Rassvet 3 satellite reportedly weighing about 370 kg — far too few for sustained connectivity but evidence of a build-up.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Constellation launch cadence is a concrete, trackable metric for when Russian deep-strike drones could gain Starlink-class control links.

insights.claim: Ukraine struck Russia's largest space communication centre at Dubna near Moscow on 22 June and a second space facility in the Vladimir region on 24 June with one-way attack drones, suggesting Ukraine treats Russian space capabilities as war-relevant targets.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A new target category: deliberate targeting of space ground segment signals Ukraine intends to pre-empt Russia closing the satcom gap.

insights.claim: Russian recruitment rates have slowed by Russia's own data while the military has announced ambitious plans to scale conventional maneuver units and dramatically expand its unmanned systems force, making the manpower equation arithmetically unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Sets up a forced choice — new incentives, alternative recruitment, or covert/overt mobilisation — each with distinct political and market consequences inside Russia.
insights.quote: The point is by Russia's own numbers, the manpower math no longer works.

insights.claim: Perun expects Russia to attempt something on manpower either in the second half of 2026 or early 2027, whether new incentives, alternative recruitment sources, or overt or covert additional mobilisation.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A dated forecast window for a politically sensitive Russian domestic event that would mark a real escalation in the Kremlin's pain tolerance.

themes.theme: Ukraine's deep strike and air-defence stretching

insights.claim: Ukraine's strategy has shifted away from Bakhmut-style attritional defence of Russian-chosen objectives toward 'fighting around the problem' — stretching Russian air defences with long and mid-range strikes and creating pressure on sectors that are not Russia's current focus.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The central strategic thesis of the episode; explains why Ukrainian territorial losses can coexist with an improving overall position.

insights.claim: Moscow's primary oil refinery is reportedly going to be offline at least through the end of 2026 and potentially into 2027 following Ukrainian long-range strikes.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Multi-quarter refinery outages near the capital are the kind of durable capacity loss that shows up in Russian domestic fuel prices and rationing.

insights.claim: Ukrainian strikes on Moscow appear to have achieved the second-order goal of pulling air defences to the capital: seven new air defence towers were identified in north and east Moscow between 19 and 21 May, a Pantsir was filmed being helicopter-installed on an apartment roof, and an S-400 battery appears to be going in near Moscow State University.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Air-defence redeployment is the measurable payoff of political-target strikes — every system in Moscow is one not covering the front.
insights.quote: every valuable Pantsir-S1 protecting Russian optics in the capital can't be protecting Russian forces elsewhere

insights.claim: Ukraine hit an electronics facility in Voronezh tied to the Russian missile industrial base with Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles, and the Progress facility in Cheboksary — critical to the Kometa-M jam-resistant antenna used in Shahed-style drones — with domestically developed Flamingo cruise missiles.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Targeting the Kometa-M antenna node attacks the input that makes Shahed drones jam-resistant — a chokepoint with outsized leverage on Russian strike effectiveness.

insights.claim: Perun cautions that the Cheboksary strike mostly destroyed the administration building rather than the production facility a few dozen to 100 metres away, warning against reading satellite damage imagery as production impact.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A discipline rule for assessing strike campaigns from open sources: which building was hit determines whether output actually falls.
insights.quote: there is going to be all the difference in the world between flattening an admin building and flattening a production facility a few dozen or 100 m away

insights.claim: Flamingo cruise missiles are appearing more frequently mixed in with drone strike packages, are hitting or nearly hitting assumed targets more regularly, and imagery suggests they may now be flying lower — which would make them harder for Russian air defences to detect.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: An improving domestic cruise missile removes Ukraine's dependence on scarce Western air-launched stocks for hardened targets.

insights.claim: Ukraine treats local power infrastructure as a niche, geographically selective target because power cuts push consumers onto backup generators, spiking diesel and gasoline demand in areas where Russian fuel logistics are already strained.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Explains why energy strikes near the front pay off militarily while equivalent strikes in central Russia do not — a targeting-efficiency rule.
insights.quote: anything that squeezes fuel availability isn't just a constraint on force mobility, it's a constraint on force combat power

themes.theme: Crimea logistics squeeze and the bridge campaign

insights.claim: Crimea is where Ukraine, not Russia, has chosen to create a problem — with the Russian governor of Crimea now declaring a state of emergency amid repeated strikes on Kerch Strait ferries, ports, loading facilities, coastal radars and oil storage.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A declared state of emergency is a rare official Russian admission of strain and the clearest confirmation the interdiction campaign is biting.

insights.claim: Perun frames oil storage tanks as a compounding target set: individually cheap to destroy and low-value, but as more are lost each remaining tank represents a larger share of capacity and the defender becomes more dependent on uninterrupted resupply.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Non-linear payoff structure means the marginal strike gets more valuable over a campaign — an argument for sustained rather than episodic targeting.

insights.claim: Russian authorities in Crimea have again halted diesel and petrol sales to civilians, pushing black or gray market prices to around three dollars a litre — about twelve dollars a gallon — with long fuel lines, tourist complaints and heavy traffic leaving via the Kerch Bridge.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer-visible fuel rationing in a flagship annexed region is the most politically legible cost of the strike campaign inside Russia.

insights.claim: Most Russian regions have now reported at least some fuel sale restrictions, and one Russian official has publicly linked this to Ukrainian strikes on refineries.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Nationwide restrictions plus official attribution mean the refinery campaign has crossed from local disruption into a systemic Russian domestic fuel problem.

insights.claim: Visually confirmed Ukrainian strikes on Russian trucks and vans have risen from roughly 20 to 30 per day a few weeks earlier to closer to 40 a day, with 193 confirmed hits over five days and 800 since early May struck more than 20 km behind the front.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A quantified, accelerating interdiction rate is the best available proxy for how fast Russian southern logistics capacity is being degraded.
insights.quote: 193 visually confirmed hits on Russian trucks and vans over the course of 5 days, with 800 in total since early May being hit more than 20 km from the front line.

insights.claim: The gap between Ukrainian claims and visual confirmation for vehicles and fuel trucks is still about 10 to 1 — roughly 40 destroyed per day visually confirmed against Ukrainian claims of 400-plus — whereas for tanks the gap has largely closed.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Where the true number sits inside that floor-to-ceiling range determines whether Russian southern logistics merely strains or actually breaks.
insights.quote: We're seeing about 40 trucks destroyed per day in the visual evidence, the Ukrainians are claiming 400 plus.

insights.claim: Footage of Ukrainian FPV strikes geolocated up to 60 km behind the front is unreasonably high quality and shows rotors, ruling out fibre optics and implying Ukraine can run FPVs at long range with a very good connection — which likely correlates with improved hit rates.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Long-range, high-bandwidth FPV control collapses the distinction between tactical and operational-depth interdiction and puts rear-area Russian traffic permanently at risk.
insights.quote: a lot of this footage is good, like unreasonably good

insights.claim: Ukraine's ePoint system aggregates for May showed no claimed increase in Russian personnel hit, but strikes beyond 50 km from the front doubled versus April and UGV logistics and evacuation missions rose about 40%.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: An independent internal Ukrainian dataset corroborating the twin shift — deeper offensive strike plus hardened own logistics — rather than relying on claims alone.

insights.claim: Cruise missiles historically failed as a bridge-interdiction tool because bridges are hard to collapse permanently, Russian engineers erect cheap pontoon replacements within days, and in extremis simply pile earth to bridge the gap.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Explains why the 2022 Kherson bridge campaign underdelivered and why exchange-rate economics, not lethality, decides interdiction outcomes.
insights.quote: As advanced and capable as modern weapons have become, against a lot of things, including top-end cruise missiles, dirt remains a fairly compelling counter.

insights.claim: The 2026 difference is a high-low munitions mix: affordable strike drones now make it economically viable to attack pontoon bridges and the traffic crossing them, removing the cost asymmetry that previously protected Russian repairs.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The key economic inflection of the episode — cheap precision mass converts previously uneconomic target classes into sustainable campaigns.
insights.quote: it's possible these pontoon bridges won't be able to rely on economics as much of an ironclad defense

insights.claim: Ukraine has struck bridges connecting Crimea to Ukraine proper as well as bridges within Crimea and across Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, in one case collapsing a road bridge onto a rail link for a two-for-one, with six hit bridges mapped along the Crimea chokepoint alone.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The density and rapid succession of hits indicate a deliberate campaign rather than opportunistic targeting, implying sustained intent and resourcing.

insights.claim: Perun's worst-case scenario for Russia is Ukraine replicating against Crimean bridges what Russia's Rubicon did to the road to Svatove during the Kursk offensive — near-continuous monitoring plus enough regular drone launches to make traffic unacceptably risky.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Persistent chokepoint denial, not one-off destruction, is the outcome that would make Russian positions in the south untenable.

insights.claim: As other road, rail and maritime links become increasingly problematic, the Kerch Strait Bridge becomes a genuinely strategic concern — a reversal of Perun's past position that its importance was overemphasised — and he expects Russia to sink everything into defending it while Ukraine takes further shots at it.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: An explicit change of view from a normally cautious analyst: the bridge is now the single highest-leverage physical node in the southern theatre.
insights.quote: the state of the bridge becomes a more and more strategic concern

themes.theme: Coercion strategy and Russian domestic tolerance

insights.claim: Ukraine's strikes on Crimea and into Russia form one coherent strategic effort to stack up costs the Russian public cannot ignore, since the MoD can falsify casualty figures but cannot hide missiles overhead, explosions and gasoline purchase restrictions.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes the deep-strike campaign as an information-and-coercion instrument targeting Kremlin negotiating incentives, not just materiel destruction.

insights.claim: Perun reports a tone shift in parts of Russian media — less triumphalism about inevitable victory, more complaints about strikes and public fretting about Crimea's future.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Media tone is an early, soft indicator of elite sentiment that would precede any Kremlin shift toward serious negotiation.

insights.claim: Perun argues the Kremlin's risk and pain tolerance is demonstrably finite — otherwise it would have declared additional mobilisation long ago and would not need Russia's sky-high internal security budget — though he stresses none of this guarantees a change in Kremlin decision-making.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The absence of mobilisation is itself evidence of a political constraint, giving a bounded model of how much pressure the Kremlin will absorb.
